title: The Untold Emotional Pain Behind Rachel Naming Ben-Oni Before She Died
paragraphs: The Untold Emotional Pain Behind Rachel Naming Ben-Oni Before She Died
There are moments in Scripture that most people read too quickly.
A sentence. A name. A burial. Then the story moves on.
But hidden inside one dying mother’s final breath is a level of emotional pain so deep that many believers have never fully stopped to feel it.
Rachel did not simply die giving birth.
She died heartbroken.
And before her soul left this world, she gave her son a name that carried the full weight of her suffering.
Most people know him as Benjamin.
But Rachel never called him that.
Her final word over her child was Ben-Oni.
And if you understand what that name truly means in Hebrew… the entire scene becomes almost unbearable.
Genesis 35:18 says:
"And it came to pass, as her soul was departing, (for she died) that she called his name Benoni: but his father called him Benjamin."
The Hebrew text reads:
וַיְהִי בְּצֵאת נַפְשָׁהּ כִּי־מֵתָה וַתִּקְרָא שְׁמוֹ בֶּן־אוֹנִי וְאָבִיו קָרָא־לוֹ בִנְיָמִין
Transliteration:
Vayehi b’tzeit nafshah ki metah vatikra sh’mo Ben-Oni; v’aviv kara lo Binyamin.
The phrase "Ben-Oni" (בֶּן־אוֹנִי) is often translated:
"Son of my sorrow"
But the depth of the Hebrew is even heavier than that.
The word "Oni" comes from the Hebrew root:
אוֹן / אָוֶן
Depending on context, it can mean: • sorrow • affliction • misery • grief • suffering • anguish • emotional exhaustion • painful labor • crushing trouble
Rachel was not naming her son after joy.
She was naming him after agony.
This was not poetic.
This was trauma speaking.
A dying woman looked at the child who cost her everything and whispered:
"You are the son of my pain."
And suddenly the story feels painfully human.
Because some of us know what it feels like to associate people with wounds.
Some people walk into our lives through heartbreak.
Some relationships cost us pieces of ourselves.
Some seasons leave scars so deep that even beautiful things become connected to suffering.
Rachel’s story is not emotionally distant.
It is terrifyingly relatable.
Especially when you realize how long Rachel had suffered before this moment.
Rachel was Jacob’s beloved.
The woman he worked fourteen years for.
The woman Scripture describes with extraordinary affection.
Genesis 29:20 says:
"And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her."
But despite being deeply loved… Rachel lived under years of silent torment.
Infertility.
Comparison.
Competition.
Emotional humiliation.
Watching her sister Leah bear child after child while her own womb remained closed.
Genesis 30:1 says:
"And when Rachel saw that she bare Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister; and said unto Jacob, Give me children, or else I die."
The Hebrew wording is emotionally explosive.
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי
Havah-li vanim, v’im-ayin metah anokhi.
Literally:
"Give me sons — and if not, I am dead."
Not physically dead.
Emotionally dead.
Internally collapsing.
Rachel was carrying years of buried grief before she ever reached Bethlehem.
People often assume biblical figures felt emotions softly.
But Scripture tells the truth about human pain.
Rachel was jealous. Rachel was desperate. Rachel was emotionally exhausted. Rachel felt forgotten. Rachel felt behind. Rachel felt broken.
And eventually God opened her womb.
She gave birth to Joseph.
Then later, during the journey near Ephrath — Bethlehem — labor became catastrophic.
Genesis 35:16-17 says:
"And they journeyed from Bethel; and there was but a little way to come to Ephrath: and Rachel travailed, and she had hard labour.
And it came to pass, when she was in hard labour, that the midwife said unto her, Fear not; thou shalt have this son also."
The Hebrew phrase for "hard labour" is:
בְּהַקְשֹׁתָהּ בְּלִדְתָּהּ
B’hakshotah b’lid’tah.
This expression communicates severe difficulty, violent pain, extreme distress.
This was not ordinary childbirth.
Rachel was dying.
And the midwife’s encouragement becomes emotionally haunting when you realize Rachel probably understood she would not survive.
"Fear not; thou shalt have this son also."
As if heaven gave her the child she longed for… at the exact cost of her own life.
Can you imagine the emotions inside her final moments?
She waited years for children.
Begged for children.
Wept for children.
Compared herself over children.
And now the second son arrives wrapped in unbearable pain.
Some mothers reading this know the terrifying nearness between life and death in childbirth.
Some people understand what it means when answered prayers arrive with suffering attached.
Because sometimes God’s blessings enter our lives through blood, tears, loss, and breaking.
That truth makes people uncomfortable.
But the Bible never hides human anguish.
And Rachel’s final act reveals something devastating:
Pain was shaping her perspective in real time.
She could not yet see beyond the suffering.
So she named the child from the place of agony.
Ben-Oni.
Son of my sorrow.
But then Jacob intervened.
Scripture says:
"But his father called him Benjamin."
In Hebrew:
בִּנְיָמִין
Binyamin.
Commonly translated:
"Son of the right hand"
The right hand in Hebrew thought symbolized: • strength • favor • authority • blessing • honor • covenant position
Rachel named him from pain.
Jacob renamed him from promise.
And suddenly the story becomes one of the most powerful spiritual pictures in all of Genesis.
Because grief wanted to define the boy.
But covenant rewrote his identity.
Somebody reading this has been living under names that pain gave you.
Failure. Rejected. Damaged. Unwanted. Too late. Too broken. Addicted. Unlovable. Forgotten.
The enemy loves naming people in moments of suffering.
Pain speaks loudly.
Trauma speaks loudly.
Depression speaks loudly.
Shame speaks loudly.
But heaven still has the authority to rename what grief tried to define.
Simon became Peter. Saul became Paul. Abram became Abraham. Jacob became Israel.
And Ben-Oni became Benjamin.
There are people smiling publicly while privately carrying identities born from wounds.
Some people were named by abusive fathers.
Some by betrayal.
Some by abandonment.
Some by church hurt.
Some by addiction.
Some by divorce.
Some by sexual trauma.
Some by failure.
Some by the worst day of their lives.
But one encounter with God can interrupt the label suffering placed on you.
This is what makes the Gospel so emotionally overwhelming.
Jesus does not merely forgive sinners.
He restores identity.
The Greek word often used for salvation in the New Testament is:
σωτηρία (sōtēria)
Which carries the idea of: • rescue • deliverance • preservation • healing • wholeness
Not just escaping hell.
Wholeness.
Christ heals what sorrow tried to rename.
Isaiah prophetically described Jesus as:
"a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief"
Isaiah 53:3.
The Hebrew says:
אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת וִידוּעַ חֹלִי
Ish mak’ovot v’yadua choli.
A man deeply familiar with pain.
Jesus understands Rachel.
He understands mothers who bury dreams.
He understands people crushed by sorrow.
He understands tears nobody else sees.
And perhaps one of the most haunting details in Rachel’s story is where she died.
Bethlehem.
The same region where centuries later another Son would be born.
One Son was named from sorrow.
Another Son would carry sorrow for the world.
Matthew later connects Rachel symbolically to grief when describing the massacre of children under Herod.
Matthew 2:18 says:
"In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children…"
Rachel became an image of grieving motherhood itself.
The woman who once cried through her own suffering became a prophetic picture of generations mourning loss.
And yet even there… God was still writing redemption.
Because Bethlehem would not only become associated with death.
It would become associated with salvation.
This is the pattern of God.
He enters places of pain and rewrites endings.
The cross itself looked like defeat.
Roman execution. Blood. Humiliation. Public shame.
But three days later resurrection exposed heaven’s deeper story.
And some of you need to hear this clearly:
Just because pain named a season does not mean pain gets the final word.
Rachel’s grief was real.
Her suffering was real.
Her tears were real.
The Bible does not minimize any of it.
But the child survived.
And Benjamin later became part of the tribes of Israel.
From Benjamin eventually came: • kings • warriors • covenant history
Even the apostle Paul identified himself as from the tribe of Benjamin.
Romans 11:1 says:
"For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin."
Imagine that.
A child once named "son of my sorrow" became part of the lineage connected to kingdom history and Gospel expansion.
That is what God does.
He brings purpose out of broken places.
Some of the people God uses most powerfully are those who survived seasons that almost emotionally buried them.
And maybe that is why this story hits so hard.
Because deep down many of us are still carrying hidden Ben-Oni moments.
Memories tied to pain.
People tied to pain.
Dreams tied to pain.
Versions of ourselves tied to pain.
But Jesus still steps into graves, trauma, shame, and sorrow saying:
"I make all things new."
Revelation 21:5.
The Greek:
Ἰδοὺ καινὰ ποιῶ πάντα
Idou kaina poiō panta.
"Behold, I am making all things new."
Not some things.
All things.
Including identities wounded by grief.
Including hearts exhausted by suffering.
Including people who secretly feel emotionally shattered.
Somebody reading this has smiled for years while carrying silent sorrow.
Somebody has attended church while internally bleeding.
Somebody has prayed while secretly wondering whether God still sees the pain.
Rachel’s story proves God does not erase human emotion from Scripture.
He preserves it.
Because He knows broken people need to see that heaven still works through shattered hearts.
And maybe tonight you need to let God rename the thing sorrow attached itself to.
Maybe your entire identity has been shaped by the darkest season you survived.
Maybe you still hear pain introducing you.
But Jesus specializes in resurrection.
Not cosmetic repair.
Resurrection.
He speaks life into dead places.
He restores what trauma distorted.
He heals what shame buried.
He redeems what suffering touched.
And one day every grieving believer will finally understand that sorrow was never the end of the story.
Be honest.
This hit harder than many expected.
Some wounds gave you names heaven never intended you to keep.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Nasasabi Tungkol sa Matinding Sakit ni Rachel Nang Pangalanan Niyang Ben-Oni ang Kanyang Anak Bago Siya Mamatay
May mga talata sa Bibliya na madalas nating madaanan nang napakabilis.
Isang pangalan. Isang pangyayari. Isang kamatayan.
Tapos tuloy agad ang kuwento.
Pero may mga talata na kapag hinayaan mong tumagos sa puso mo… babaguhin ka nila.
At isa rito ang huling salita ni Rachel habang siya ay namamatay.
Hindi lang basta namatay si Rachel habang nanganganak.
Namatay siyang wasak.
At bago tuluyang humiwalay ang kanyang kaluluwa sa kanyang katawan, binigyan niya ng pangalan ang kanyang anak mula sa pinakamalalim na sugat ng kanyang puso.
Kilala natin siya bilang Benjamin.
Pero hindi iyon ang pangalang unang ibinigay ni Rachel.
Ang huling pangalan na binigkas niya ay:
Ben-Oni.
At kapag naintindihan mo kung gaano kabigat ang ibig sabihin nito sa Hebrew… mararamdaman mong parang may humahawak sa dibdib mo.
Genesis 35:18:
"At nang naghihingalo na siya, sapagkat siya’y namatay, ay pinanganlan niya ang bata ng Benoni: datapuwa't tinawag siya ng kaniyang ama na Benjamin."
Sa Hebrew:
וַיְהִי בְּצֵאת נַפְשָׁהּ כִּי־מֵתָה וַתִּקְרָא שְׁמוֹ בֶּן־אוֹנִי וְאָבִיו קָרָא־לוֹ בִנְיָמִין
Transliteration:
Vayehi b’tzeit nafshah ki metah vatikra sh’mo Ben-Oni; v’aviv kara lo Binyamin.
Karaniwang isinasalin ang “Ben-Oni” bilang:
“Anak ng aking kalungkutan.”
Pero mas mabigat pa roon ang tunay nitong diwa.
Ang salitang “Oni” ay mula sa Hebrew root na:
אוֹן / אָוֶן
Na maaaring mangahulugan ng:
• paghihirap • matinding dalamhati • emosyonal na pagod • pagdurusa • affliction • misery • agony • crushing sorrow
Hindi pinangalanan ni Rachel ang kanyang anak mula sa saya.
Pinangalanan niya ito mula sa sakit.
Mula sa trauma.
Mula sa paghihingalo.
Isang ina na unti-unti nang namamatay ang tumingin sa kanyang anak at para bang bumulong:
“Ikaw ang anak ng aking sakit.”
At doon nagiging sobrang totoo ang kuwento.
Dahil marami sa atin ang may mga bagay na konektado sa sakit.
May mga alaalang hindi natin kayang balikan nang hindi umiiyak.
May mga tao tayong minahal na iniwan tayong wasak.
May mga panalangin tayong nasagot… pero may kapalit na sugat.
At iyon mismo ang nangyari kay Rachel.
Bago pa man siya makarating sa Bethlehem, matagal na siyang sugatan.
Si Rachel ang pinakamamahal ni Jacob.
Siya ang babaeng pinagtrabahuhan ni Jacob nang labing-apat na taon.
Genesis 29:20:
"At naglingkod si Jacob na dahil kay Rachel ay pitong taon; at naging parang ilang araw lamang sa kaniya, dahil sa pagibig niya sa kaniya."
Mahal siya.
Pero kahit mahal siya… hindi ibig sabihin noon ay hindi siya nasasaktan.
Dahil taon-taon niyang pinapanood si Leah na magkaanak habang siya ay baog.
Taon-taon niyang kinukumpara ang sarili niya.
Taon-taon siyang umiiyak sa katahimikan.
Genesis 30:1:
"Bigyan mo ako ng mga anak, o kung hindi ay mamamatay ako."
Sa Hebrew:
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי
Havah-li vanim, v’im-ayin metah anokhi.
Literal:
“Bigyan mo ako ng mga anak — kung hindi, para na rin akong patay.”
Hindi ito simpleng drama.
Ito ay sigaw ng isang pusong pagod na pagod na.
May mga taong nakangiti sa labas pero matagal nang patay ang loob sa loob.
At iyon si Rachel.
Kaya nang sa wakas ay buksan ng Diyos ang kanyang sinapupunan… dumating nga ang pagpapala… pero dumating din ang matinding sakit.
Genesis 35:16-17:
"At sila'y naglakbay mula sa Bethel… at si Rachel ay naghirap sa panganganak.
At nang siya'y mahirapan sa panganganak, sinabi sa kaniya ng hilot, Huwag kang matakot; sapagka't magkakaroon ka rin ng anak na lalake."
Ang Hebrew phrase para sa “nahirapan sa panganganak” ay:
בְּהַקְשֹׁתָהּ בְּלִדְתָּהּ
B’hakshotah b’lid’tah.
Hindi ito ordinaryong labor pain.
Ito ay matinding paghihirap.
Violently painful.
Life-threatening.
At marahil alam na ni Rachel na hindi na siya makakaligtas.
Kaya sobrang bigat ng sinabi ng hilot:
“Huwag kang matakot; magkakaroon ka rin ng anak.”
Parang ibinigay ng langit ang matagal na niyang hinihintay… kasabay ng pagkuha ng kanyang buhay.
Ilang taon niyang ipinagdasal ang anak na iyon.
Ilang gabi siyang umiyak para doon.
Ilang beses niyang kinuwestiyon ang sarili niya.
At ngayon dumating nga ang bata… pero kasabay ng kanyang kamatayan.
May mga tao rito na naiintindihan ang pakiramdam na iyon.
Na minsan ang answered prayer ay may kasamang sugat.
Na minsan ang blessing ay dumadaan muna sa pagdurugo.
Hindi tinatago ng Bibliya ang sakit ng tao.
At iyon ang dahilan kung bakit napakatotoo nito.
Sa huling sandali ni Rachel, ang sakit ang nagsasalita.
Kaya tinawag niya siyang:
Ben-Oni.
Anak ng aking dalamhati.
Pero biglang may ginawa si Jacob.
Sabi ng Bibliya:
“Ngunit tinawag siya ng kanyang ama na Benjamin.”
Sa Hebrew:
בִּנְיָמִין
Binyamin.
Ibig sabihin:
“Anak ng kanang kamay.”
At sa kultura ng Hebrew, ang “kanang kamay” ay simbolo ng:
• lakas • pabor • karangalan • awtoridad • pagpapala
Napakalalim nito.
Pinangalanan siya ni Rachel mula sa sakit.
Pero pinangalanan siya ni Jacob mula sa pangako.
At dito pumapasok ang napakalalim na mensahe ng Diyos.
Dahil maraming tao ang nabubuhay gamit ang pangalan na ibinigay ng trauma.
“Wala kang kwenta.”
“Marumi ka.”
“Sirang-sira ka na.”
“Hindi ka na magbabago.”
“Hindi ka na kayang mahalin.”
“Palpak ka.”
“Hindi ka sapat.”
Maraming tao ang ipinakilala ng sakit.
Pero may kapangyarihan ang Diyos na baguhin ang pangalan na ibinigay ng sugat.
Si Abram naging Abraham. Si Jacob naging Israel. Si Simon naging Peter. Si Saul naging Paul.
At si Ben-Oni naging Benjamin.
May mga taong tahimik na lumalaban araw-araw habang dinadala ang identity na nilikha ng trauma.
At marahil kaya sobrang bigat ng kuwentong ito… dahil marami sa atin ang may sariling “Ben-Oni” moments.
Mga memoryang konektado sa sakit.
Mga panahong halos sumira sa atin.
Mga gabing umiyak tayo nang walang nakakaalam.
Pero ang ebanghelyo ni Cristo ay hindi lang tungkol sa kapatawaran.
Ito ay tungkol sa restoration.
Sa Greek, ang salitang madalas gamitin para sa “kaligtasan” ay:
σωτηρία (sōtēria)
Na hindi lang ibig sabihin ay “ligtas.”
Kasama rito ang:
• healing • wholeness • deliverance • rescue • restoration
Si Jesus ay hindi lang namatay para patawarin ka.
Namatay Siya para ibalik kung sino ka talaga sa mata ng Diyos.
Isaiah 53:3:
"Lalaki ng kapanglawan at bihasa sa pagdadalamhati."
Sa Hebrew:
אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת וִידוּעַ חֹלִי
Ish mak’ovot v’yadua choli.
Ibig sabihin:
Isang taong lubos na nakakakilala ng sakit.
Naiintindihan ni Jesus ang pagdurusa ni Rachel.
Naiintindihan Niya ang mga pusong tahimik na umiiyak.
Naiintindihan Niya ang mga taong pagod nang magpanggap na okay.
At napakalalim din na si Rachel ay namatay malapit sa Bethlehem.
Dahil makalipas ang maraming taon… isa pang Anak ang isisilang sa Bethlehem.
Ang isang anak ay pinangalanan mula sa kalungkutan.
Pero ang isa pang Anak… dadalhin ang kalungkutan ng buong mundo.
Si Jesus.
At doon mo makikita ang pattern ng Diyos.
Hindi Siya umiiwas sa lugar ng sakit.
Pumapasok Siya roon.
At binabago Niya ang ending.
Ang krus ay mukhang pagkatalo.
Dugo. Kahihiyan. Pagdurusa.
Pero pagkatapos ng tatlong araw… dumating ang resurrection.
At may mga taong kailangang marinig ito ngayon:
Hindi porket sakit ang nagbigay ng pangalan sa season mo… ibig sabihin sakit na ang may huling salita.
May plano pa rin ang Diyos.
May redemption pa rin.
May healing pa rin.
May resurrection pa rin.
At ang batang minsang tinawag na “anak ng aking kalungkutan”… naging bahagi ng kasaysayan ng Israel.
Mula sa tribo ni Benjamin nagmula ang mga mandirigma, mga lider, at maging si apostle Paul.
Isipin mo iyon.
Ang batang ipinanganak sa matinding sakit ay ginamit pa rin ng Diyos sa mas malaking layunin.
At baka iyon din ang ginagawa ng Diyos sa buhay mo ngayon.
Baka ang season na halos sumira sa’yo… iyon pa ang gagamitin Niya para magligtas ng iba.
Baka ang sugat na pilit mong tinatago… iyon pa ang magiging testimony mo.
Baka hindi pa tapos ang Diyos sa kuwento mo.
Maging totoo ka.
May mga sugat na matagal nating tinatago.
May mga pangalang ibinigay sa’yo ng sakit na hindi kailanman intensyon ng langit na manatili sa’yo.
